newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo copper guru serious and quiet.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo copper guru serious and quiet.

text.p: In the rough world of commodity trading, he was known as "Mr Copper", a feared figure in the metal markets.

But for those who have known him for many years, disgraced Sumitomo Corp trader Yasuo Hamanaka is a quiet family man, not at all the kind of person who would carry out the biggest financial fraud in history.
He goes on trial on Monday on charges of fraud and forgery, accused of using fraudulent accounts to trade copper without his company"s knowledge. He faces up to 15 years in prison.
Before he was fired in June 1996, Hamanaka was considered the most influential and controversial player in the world metal market.

His lifestyle did not match his high-rolling professional image, however. His two-storey house in the city of Kawasaki, on the outskirts of Tokyo, is only average in a neighbourhood populated by mid-level office workers rather than financial superstars.
Long-time friends said that as a student Hamanaka was a serious and shy person who loved reading the works of British philosopher John Stuart Mill.
"Yasuo was a really serious and gentle student, and never gambled at cards. I can"t believe the allegation he was a rogue trader," a former classmate said.
"Even if Sumitomo"s allegations are true, I think he has done everything for the sake of the company," she said.
He began his career in 1970 after graduating from Tokyo"s Seikei University, a private college that is popular but not especially prestigious.
It was a time of stormy student protests around the nation, but Hamanaka did not get involved.
Even though Sumitomo says he racked up losses of $2.6 billion, Hamanaka is remembered as more interested in political theory than hard numbers.
"I remember Yasuo was not good at mathematics then and rather preferred social sciences," another classmate said.
His father Eiji Hamanaka, who died about 10 years ago, was once a high-ranking official of the National Police Agency, and his grandfather Shoroku Aikawa was the Health and Welfare Minister in 1945.
After joining Sumitomo 27 years ago, Hamanaka worked at its inspection department for years. In 1974 he married Yoko Hattori, then an assistant for Hamanaka at that section.
He and his wife now have two children. Their daughter graduated from a women"s junior college last spring and their son is still at high school.
The former classmates agree that Hamanaka became increasingly busy from 1975, when he was assigned to Sumitomo"s non-ferrous metals department.
"When we had drinks occasionally, Yasuo talked about how exciting the metals business is," a third classmate said.
"But I haven"t received any New Year card from Yasuo in the last three to four years, and was wondering what happened to him," he said.
